questions.question: In 1784, who discovered the composition of water through his experiment with hydrogen and oxygen?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Henry Cavendish**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **In 1784, British scientist Henry Cavendish **presented his findings on water's composition to the Royal Society.
 
• Cavendish conducted a pioneering laboratory experiment where he successfully synthesized water by **combining hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio**, thereby demonstrating that water is a compound.
 
• Henry Cavendish FRS, an English natural philosopher and scientist, made significant contributions to experimental and theoretical chemistry and physics. He is renowned for his discovery of hydrogen, initially termed "inflammable air."
 
• In his 1766 paper titled "On Factitious Airs," Cavendish described the density of inflammable air, which formed water upon combustion.
 
• Antoine Lavoisier later adopted Cavendish's experiment and coined the name "hydrogen" for the element.
 
• Cavendish was widely respected for his meticulous precision and accuracy in various research areas, including the composition of atmospheric air, the properties of different gases, water synthesis, laws governing electrical attraction and repulsion, a mechanical theory of heat, and calculations related to the density and mass of the Earth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Herbert Charles Brown**, an American chemist, was awarded the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his pioneering research on organoboranes.
 
• **Joseph Priestley, **an English polymath, was known for his contributions to chemistry, philosophy, theology, education, and political theory.
 
• **John Dalton**, an English scientist, made significant contributions to chemistry, physics, and meteorology, particularly for his groundbreaking work on atomic theory.

questions.question: Who explained the structure of protein?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is **__Pauling and Corey__.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Linus Pauling** is recognized for successfully predicting regular **protein secondary structures **based on** hydrogen bonding,** an idea originally proposed by **William Astbury**.
 
• **Pauling and Corey** formulated a model for the conformation of **fibrous proteins called beta-keratins**, where the polypeptide adopts an extended zig-zag configuration rather than a coil, such as in the alpha-helix.
 
• All proteins in the human body can be synthesized from permutations of just **20 amino acids**.
 
• There are seven primary types of proteins: antibodies, contractile proteins, enzymes, hormonal proteins, structural proteins, storage proteins, and transport proteins.
 
• A protein molecule is composed of a lengthy chain of these amino acids, each linked to its adjacent amino acid through a covalent peptide bond.
 
• Hence, proteins are also referred to as polypeptides. Each type of protein possesses a distinctive sequence of amino acids, which remains identical from one molecule to another.
 
• Numerous proteins with diverse functions are known, each characterized by its specific amino acid sequence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Emil Fischer**, a German organic chemist, is credited with the** discovery of caffeine **and other related purines.
 
• Additionally, he conducted extensive research on the molecular structures of sugars and proteins, earning him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1902.
 
• **Proteins** are comprised of amino acids, with **21 naturally occurring variants**.
 
• Secondary protein structures are stabilized by hydrogen bonding. The characteristics of protein strands vary depending on the type of hydrogen bonding present, with two common types being the alpha helix and beta sheet.
 
• The alpha helix is a right-handed coiled secondary protein structure, where the substituents of the amino acids extend outward.
 
• Hydrogen bonds form between the carbonyl oxygen and the four NH bonds below it, contributing to the stability of the helix.

questions.question: The structure that produces and holds sperm cells in bryophytes (non-vascular plants) and ferns is called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**antheridium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Antheridium:-**

 
 
• **The structure that produces and holds sperm cells in bryophytes (non-vascular plants) and ferns is called an antheridium.**
 
• It is a small, multicellular structure that typically consists of a jacket of sterile cells surrounding a cluster of sperm cells.
 
• The sperm cells, also known as antherozoids, are flagellated, meaning they have tails that allow them to swim.
 
• When the antheridium matures, the jacket ruptures, releasing the sperm cells into the surrounding water.
 
• The sperm cells then swim towards the archegonia, which are the structures that produce egg cells in bryophytes and ferns. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Megasporangia:-**

 
 
• **These are structures that produce megaspores, which are large, haploid spores that develop into female gametophytes. **
 
• Female gametophytes are the haploid phase of the plant life cycle and produce egg cells.
 
• Megasporangia are typically found on the sporophytes, which are the diploid phase of the plant life cycle and produce spores.
 
 
 
• **Archegonia:-**
 
 
• These are structures that produce egg cells.
 
• **They are also found on the gametophytes. Archegonia are typically flask-shaped and have a neck, a venter, and an egg cell. **
 
• When a sperm cell swims down the neck of an archegonium and fertilizes the egg cell, a zygote is formed. The zygote develops into a sporophyte.
 
 
 
• **Protonema:-**
 
 
• It is the first stage of the life cycle of a non-vascular plant.
 
• **It is a filamentous, thread-like structure that develops from a germinating spore. **
 
• The protonema is responsible for anchorage and absorption of water and nutrients. It also produces buds that develop into gametophytes.

questions.question: What are the thin filamentous extensions that the motile bacterial cells have from their cell wall called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Flagella**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The thin filamentous extensions that motile bacterial cells have from their cell wall are called **Flagella**.
 
• Flagella are lash-like appendages that protrude from the cell body of certain prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, providing the means for locomotion.
 
• They are essential for the motility of bacteria, allowing them to move toward favorable environments or away from harmful ones.
 
• Flagella are composed of the protein flagellin and are powered by a rotary engine at the base of the flagellum.
 
• They are different from other cell appendages like pili and fimbriae, which are primarily involved in attachment rather than movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pili** are hair-like structures on the surface of bacterial cells that are involved in attachment to surfaces and in the exchange of genetic material during conjugation.
 
• **Fimbriae** are similar to pili but are usually shorter and more numerous, primarily aiding in the attachment to surfaces and to other cells.
 
• **Lamellae** are thin layers, plates, or disks in various biological contexts but are not related to bacterial motility.

questions.question: Identify the pigment that gives blood its colour.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Haemoglobin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hemoglobin **is the pigment responsible for the **red colour of blood**.
 
• It's a **protein** found in **red blood cells**.
 
• **Hemoglobin** carries **oxygen** from the **lungs to body tissues** and returns **carbon dioxide** to the **lungs**.
 
• The **iron-containing heme group** within **haemoglobin** gives blood its r**ed colour**. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ferritin**

 
 
• **Ferritin** is a **protein** that **stores iron in cells**.
 
• It helps **regulate iron levels **in **the body**.
 
• Composed of **24 subunits** forming a **spherical structure**.
 
• Measurement of **ferritin levels in blood indicates iron status**.
 
• **Low levels** may indicate** iron deficiency**; **high levels**,** iron overload **or other conditions.
 
 
 
• **Chlorophyll**
 
 
• **Green pigment** found in **chloroplasts** of **plants and algae**.
 
• Essential for **photosynthesis**, converting **sunlight into chemical energ**y.
 
• Absorbs light in **blue and red wavelengths**, **reflecting green light**.
 
• Captures light energy to synthesize **carbohydrates** from **CO2 and water**.
 
• **Molecular structure** includes a **porphyrin ring** with a **magnesium ion**, giving it its **green colour**.
 
 
 
• **Xanthophyll**
 
 
• **Yellow pigment **found in **plants and algae**.
 
• Contributes to **leaf colouration**, **especially in autumn**.
 
• Doesn't directly participate in **photosynthesis**.
 
• Helps dissipate excess **light energy, protecting chlorophyll**.
 
• Also provides **photoprotection against UV radiation.**

questions.question: To what phylum does a blood sucking leech belong?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Annelida**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Leeches belong to the phylum **Annelida**.
 
• Annelida is a phylum of segmented worms, which also includes earthworms and polychaetes.
 
• Leeches are characterized by their segmented bodies and the presence of suckers at both ends, which they use for attachment and feeding.
 
• They are mostly found in freshwater environments, but some species are terrestrial or marine.
 
• Leeches are known for their role in medicine, particularly in ancient times and even today in microsurgery for their blood-sucking capabilities and anticoagulant properties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The name **Annelida** is derived from the Latin word "anellus," meaning little ring, which refers to the ring-like segments that make up their bodies.
 
• Leeches have been used in medicinal practices for centuries, especially for their ability to draw blood and reduce blood clotting.
 
• In modern medicine, leeches are sometimes used in reconstructive surgery to help stimulate blood circulation in reattached tissues.
 
• Leeches produce a substance called hirudin, which is a powerful anticoagulant, preventing blood from clotting during feeding.
 
• The study of annelids is important in understanding soil health and ecosystem dynamics, as many annelids play crucial roles in soil aeration and nutrient cycling.

questions.question: Who was the first ecologist to describe the specific shape of eco-trophic interactions,Which he called the pyramid of numbers, in the 1920s?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Charles Elton**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Charles Elton** was the **first ecologist** to describe the specific shape of eco-trophic interactions, Which he called the pyramid of numbers, in the 1920s.
 
• He was an esteemed English zoologist and animal ecologist, is credited with pioneering the concept of the ecological pyramid in 1927.
 
• Elton also introduced the term "pyramid of numbers" to elucidate the phenomenon where lower trophic levels typically harbor a greater number of individuals compared to higher trophic levels.
 
• Ecological pyramids serve as graphical representations delineating the interrelationships among different organisms across various trophic levels.
 
• These pyramids elucidate the relative quantities of diverse parameters across trophic levels, encompassing factors such as the abundance of organisms, energy flow, and biomass distribution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ernst Haeckel,** a renowned German zoologist and evolutionist, staunchly advocated for Darwinism and put forth innovative concepts regarding the evolutionary ancestry of humans.
 
• **Howard Thomas Odum,** commonly referred to as H. T. Odum, was an influential American ecologist celebrated for his groundbreaking contributions to ecosystem ecology. He also proposed thought-provoking extensions to the laws of thermodynamics, drawing from his insights into general systems theory.
 
• **E.O. Wilson**, an esteemed American biologist, is widely acclaimed as the foremost expert on ants globally. His extensive research and expertise have significantly advanced our understanding of ant behavior and ecology.

questions.question: Which Nobel Laureate conducted an experiment in the late 19th century and observed that a glass tube filled with a low-pressure gas emitted radiation when a voltage was applied between two metal plates?

• **Nobel Laureate Philipp Lenard** conducted an experiment in the late 19th century and observed that a glass tube filled with a **low-pressure gas emitted** radiation when a voltage was applied between two metal plates.
 
• He observed that when a voltage was applied between two metal plates inside the tube, the gas emitted radiation.
 
• This phenomenon was significant as it contributed to the understanding of the interaction between electricity and matter, leading to advancements in the field of physics.
 
• Lenard's experiments laid the groundwork for further research into the properties of radiation and its implications for the field of science.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Victor Francis Hess**, an Austrian-born physicist, shared the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1936 with Carl D. Anderson of the United States. They were recognized for the discovery of cosmic rays, which are high-energy radiation originating from outer space.
 
• **Paul Adrien Maurice **was an English physicist renowned for his contributions to the development of quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics. He is widely regarded as one of the founders of these fields.
 
• **Hideki Yukawa **was a Japanese theoretical physicist and the first Japanese scientist to receive a Nobel Prize. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his prediction of the existence of the pi meson, also known as the pion.

questions.question: What do you call the fluid matrix filling in the cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Cytoplasm.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cytoplasm** is a** gelatinous fluid **occupying the **space within a cell,** which serves as the region between the **plasma membrane and the nucleus**.
 
• It encompasses both the** cytosol,** a semi-fluid portion, and various organelles suspended within it.
 
• Notably,** prokaryotic cells **lack membrane-bound organelles characteristic of eukaryotic cells, such as mitochondria or endoplasmic reticulum.
 
• Instead, their cytoplasm contains various structures essential for cellular functions, albeit without the distinct membrane boundaries seen in eukaryotic organelles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ribosomes** are large ribonucleoprotein complexes found ubiquitously in all cells. Comprising both RNA and proteins, ribosomes play a crucial role in translating genetic information stored in mRNA into polypeptide chains.
 
• **Plasmids** are small, extrachromosomal DNA molecules present within a cell, physically distinct from the chromosomal DNA and capable of replicating independently. They often carry non-essential genes that may confer advantages such as antibiotic resistance.
 
• Discovered in 1897 by Italian physician Camillo Golgi, the Golgi complex is a cellular organelle consisting of five to eight flattened membrane-bound sacs known as cisternae. It plays a vital role in processing, modifying, and packaging proteins and lipids for transport within the cell or secretion outside the cell.

questions.question: During which phase of the cell cycle does metabolic changes assemble the cytoplasmic material required for mitosis and cytokinesis?
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is** __G2 Phase__.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The G2 phase of the cell cycle **involves metabolic changes that assemble **cytoplasmic materials **necessary for** mitosis and cytokinesis**.
 
• This phase is followed by the **M phase**, where **nuclear division (mitosis) **is followed by **cell division (cytokinesis)**.
 
• Eukaryotic cells undergo a series of stages collectively known as the cell cycle, which includes** two gap phases (G1 and G2)**, an **S phase (synthesis)** where genetic material is duplicated, and an M phase where mitosis partitions the genetic material and the cell divides.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

__
 
• During **mitosis, chromosomes **replicated during the **S phase **are divided to ensure that each daughter cell receives a copy of **every chromosome**.
 
• This process results in the production of **two daughter cells **with the same genetic component as the parent cell.
 
• In actively dividing animal cells, the entire process typically takes about one hour.
 
• The final cellular division results in the formation of two new cells.
 
• Following mitosis is Meiosis II, where Meiosis I is a reduction division resulting in haploid cells with one copy of each chromosome.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **G1 phase:** During this phase, metabolic changes prepare the cell for division. At a specific point called the restriction point, the cell commits to division and enters the S phase.
 
• **S phase:** In this phase, DNA synthesis occurs, resulting in the replication of the genetic material. Each chromosome now consists of two sister chromatids.
 
• **G2 phase: **Metabolic changes in this phase assemble the cytoplasmic materials necessary for mitosis and cytokinesis.
 
• **M phase:** This phase involves nuclear division (mitosis) followed by cell division (cytokinesis).

questions.question: Which membrane-bound cell organelle consisting of a small sac-like structure surrounded by single membranes serves as the cell's digestive system, allowing material taken from outside the cell to degrade and digest obsolete components of the cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lysosome**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ​Lysosome:

 
 
• Lysosomes are an important cell organelle found within eukaryotic animal cells.
 
• Due to their peculiar function, they are also known as the “suicide bags” of the cell.
 
• Lysosomes work as the waste-discarding structures of the cell by processing undesirable materials and degrading them, both from the exterior of the cell and waste constituents inside the cell.
 
• But sometimes, the digestive enzymes may end up damaging the lysosomes themselves, and this can cause the cell to die.
 
• This is termed autolysis, where **“auto” means “self” and “lysis” means “the disintegration of the cell by the destruction of its cell membrane“**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Peroxisomes:

 
 
• It is a microbody.
 
• In-plant it helps in photorespiration.
 
• In animals concerned with peroxide metabolism.
 
 
 
• Glyoxysomes: These are the **special type of peroxisomes found in plants & some fungi.**
 
• **Polysome:** Many **ribosomes may associate with a single mRNA** to form **multiple copies of a polypeptide simultaneously**.
 
 
• Such strings of ribosomes are termed as **Polysome**.
